Sentence: The paper conflates two separate questions: a) Does the visual information in multimodal models guard against reporting bias, and b) Does more-visually grounded text suffer less from reporting bias than less-visually grounded text?

By only comparing pretrained BERT vs Oscar, the experiments cannot separate questions, and are in danger of drawing unmerited conclusions (e.g. L504 'concludes that ... images+text outperform text-only models': but how well does text-only Oscar perform here?).
Disentangling them would require training a BERT model on Oscar's text data (maybe the model alluded to in preliminary experiments, L354?).
The 'distilled' model is close to this, but the discussion around this model is unclear.
Oscar (and distilled BERT) are trained on COCO, which is part of Visual Genome.
There is therefore a 'training on test' problem here, making it difficult to separate the effect of adding the visual modality vs matching the test distribution better than Wikipedia.

In fairness, Section 5.3 and Table 5 compare VG-trained Oscar with (probably) VG-free CLIP and do not see any large differences between the two, indicating it’s not the VG-in-training that drives differences between BERT and the multimodal models (more likely genre/domain differences, or the actual visual inputs).
The paper is missing discussion of early related work that used e.g. McRae norms; e.g. Silberer et al (2013) and references therein.
It would be useful to check whether the McRae norms agreed with the extracted VG properties.
The McRae dataset is smaller than the extracted VG dataset in this paper, but models might do better or show different patterns for the more salient concepts included in McRae.
The term 'common sense' is currently overused and underdefined in NLP.
The discussion on L113-120 about 'visual commonsense' vs 'stereotypic visual attributes' is explicit about the context in this paper; reconsider whether 'visual commonsense' is the best terminology.
Do all the models use the same tokenisation?
The 'mask first token' methodology (Footnote 4) would lead to better MLM results for models with finer-grained/shorter subwords if tokenisation is not controlled for.
Why does soft prompt tuning have a huge effect on Color (~20-30 points) but much less for other attribute types?
Figure 2/451: The Vokenization model has the second highest correlation gap between Wikipedia and COCO, after BERT — if true, does this imply vokenisation doesn’t work?
In Table 3, Column Color, Bert_L has the same values for Tune=N/Y. Is this a typo or coincidence?
A.2 Table 9: is it with or without tuning?
The appendix figures could use more explanation (e.g., what are the color indices in Figures 8,9; what are the subjects in Figures 6,7).
It would help to show high/low correlation subjects (Table 11) for Single/Multi/Any subjects separately.
Section 4.2 (Elicitation methods) includes paragraphs on soft prompt tuning and knowledge distillation, which is confusing.
My main concerns are the lack of novelty and proper comparison with a previous study.
